items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: This repository provides three physics-based datasets for developing and evaluating surrogate models to identify the seismic failure modes (SFMs) of coastal reinforced concrete bridge bents supported by pile-group foundations under combined scour and corrosion. Each sample contains 20 input variables: 17 structural and geotechnical parameters, scour depth, and the corrosion levels of longitudinal and transverse column reinforcement. The output is one of three SFMs: column flexural failure (CFF), foundation flexural failure (FFF), or column shear-associated failure (CSF). These labels are determined through nonlinear finite element analysis and code-based shear capacity calculations. The datasets support reproducible surrogate model development and subsequent life-cycle probabilistic assessment of SFMs and their transitions in deteriorating coastal bridge bents.
items.title: Seismic Failure Mode Datasets for Coastal Pile-Group-Supported Bridge Bents Subjected to Scour and Corrosion

items.summary: Machine-readable evidence and analysis code for a PRISMA-2020 systematic review of fairness in histopathology AI. Contents. (i) The dual-coded, adjudicated extraction table for the 88-study analytical corpus (61 from the main search, 17 from the demographic-term update, 2 retrieved in October 2026, 2 suggested in peer review, 1 candidate resolved on full text and 5 from a re-screen of the keyword-filtered records; 89 records, one conference abstract linked to its journal paper; the earlier 62- and 79-study tables are kept alongside), with the pre-pass snapshots and the script that applies the October 2026 revisions, with the raw multi-coder outputs and inter-coder agreement statistics; (ii) the screening, de-duplication and post-hoc eligibility-audit logs; (iii) adjudicated QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias judgements for all 88 studies, with per-coder judgements for the original 62; (iv) the full consensus-endorsement coding pipeline — screened review pools, the pre-specified random sample (n=30, seed 20260913), the coding specification, two independent coder passes, disagreements and their adjudication, and tallies with Wilson 95% confidence intervals; (v) the 39-dataset demographic-metadata audit; and (vi) a claim-by-claim statistics register mapping every reported number to its source rows, together with the code that produces each value. Full texts of the reviewed papers are not included, for copyright reasons. Code is licensed MIT; data tables are licensed CC BY 4.0. A SHA-256 manifest ( MANIFEST.sha256 ) covers every file in the package. This package is a working-tree snapshot of the manuscript as of 18 October 2026 (62 pp main + 45 pp supplementary). Manuscript v0.6.10 (31 October 2026). Peer-review revision. One coded row corrected ( asadiaghbolagh2024learning HED is positive: the archived full text gives pleural 76.80 vs 76.70 and describes it as similar, while 66.60 does not occur in the source) and one recoded ( song2020automatic is workflow_only because it reports no comparator). Data augmentation is now 8 positive of 13 bias-endpoint studies (7 cross-site), 4 mixed, 1 negative, 2 no-endpoint, 62% (36-82); the family grade is unchanged (Mixed). Table 3, Figure 3, both sensitivity tables, the supplementary evidence and adjudication tables, the evidence TSV and the adjudication log were regenerated; statistics register rows V6-1 and V6-2. Twenty peer-review comment groups were also applied (abstract/Results/Conclusion fairness-metric qualifier; Methods 2.9 screening chronology; Methods 2.5; Methods 2.7 row arithmetic and multiplicity; Introduction novelty paragraph citing Xu et al. 2024; Discussion metadata-dependence sentence and denominators; Conclusion CIs). No headline statistic changed (88 studies, 89 records). Manuscript v0.6.9 (30 October 2026). Response to the fifth deep review (every comment except the human audit, which will not be performed); no coded value, count, grade or headline statistic changed. Fixed: the search chronology in the Methods (the model account covers the March 2026 round onward; the January and June 2024 rounds' tooling is unrecorded); the 62-record follow-up arithmetic (2 + 12 + 48) and the partition of the 16 re-screen candidates; 61 studies in 62 records in the PRISMA flow with the F6 exclusion code defined; the 79-record denominator for the risk-of-bias disagreements and the four-positive feature-level harmonization wording; the non-AI exception now discloses the bovine control tissue of the laboratory stain audit (denominators unchanged); CohortFinder's held-out test set described and the Puerto-Rico prostate validation cited in Section 3; FLEX's 0.140 to 0.085 disparity reduction attributed to its C-LUAD-EGFR task and AIDA given for all four cohorts; the eleven no-bias-endpoint family rows named; D6's expectation under noisy uniform attention with its averaging and subgroup-count definitions; FlexFair's criteria; ten bibliography entries. items.summary: Everything needed to redo the two analyses reported in the Technical Note named in the title, and nothing else. What is here the secondary analysis of published length-resolved binding: the contract frozen before any test statistic was computed and its two dated amendments, the resampling of the source's own trimmed-mean procedure, the anchored and anchor-free tests, the post-hoc robustness check across five normalisation variants, the superseded first run kept so the correction stays visible, and the figure generator; the two propositions behind the simulation and the script that checks both against the stored benchmark, per replicate; the simulated measurement study it checks: frozen primary and stress designs, the finite-chain engine, 7,200 simulated datasets under seven observation operators reported as all 302,400 planned rows including the undefined, outside-window and non-identified slots, an independent validator, the stress results, five focused tests, an 83-file manifest and a dependency lock; an 80-value subset of the Source Data for Fig. 2B/C of Sheikh et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 3617 (2022), with its sheet coordinates. These values keep the original article's CC BY 4.0 licence and attribution; the rest of the archive is under the MIT licence in LICENSE. Reproducing The added analysis runs from the archive root with the standard library plus NumPy; the README gives the four commands. It was re-run on an interpreter far older than the one that produced the shipped results (Python 3.7.6 with NumPy 1.19.1, against 3.13.17 with 2.5.3): the proposition checks were identical in all 520 compared values apart from the recorded environment, and three bootstrap interval endpoints differed in their last digits, by at most 1.5e-11. Figures redraw with the same layout; their byte sequences depend on which sans-serif face the host has. The base study's own replay script requires bit equality and returns a failure on Linux, where ten of its twenty tables differ in their last digits. What is deliberately not here the manuscript text; the original publisher workbook of Sheikh et al. and every panel of it other than the 80 values used; historical MCMC traces and the exploratory transcript analysis of an earlier, separate study, which this work does not use; correspondence and author-only files. REDACTION.md lists the three files whose description of the work was restated for publication, with the digest before and after; no number, method, decision rule or result changed. Scope Synthetic counts are idealised events, not biological replicates. The site-equivalent pool is not an alpha-dystroglycan molecule count, glycan mass, antibody intensity or muscle force. The published array values are technical replicates of one experiment, and the source states no independent experiments. No real assay's detection ceiling or recovery function is measured anywhere in this archive.

items.summary: Surface code decoders like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) can also be used to estimate or bound the probability of a logical failure conditioned on the error syndrome commonly called ``soft outputs''. Estimates like the complementary gap of a matching, or others like the ``cluster gap'' are used to produce high fidelity magic states via post-selection. They are also helpful in reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant computation via code concatenation schemes like yoked surface codes. In this work we provide techniques to tightly lower bound the complementary gap of a rotated surface code syndrome block and provide fast parallel algorithms for computing this lower bound efficiently. Our algorithms run in real time for the moderate distances and reasonable physical noise rates required by these applications. We achieve latencies of the order of one to tens of microseconds on sufficiently fast CPU cores.
items.title: Fast Bounds on Matching Decoder Soft Output for the Surface Code

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. Data and code supporting the article "Revoking Access Does Not Revoke Knowledge: Enforcing Mid-Task Permission Changes in AI agents:

items.summary: 50/60 MISSION RELIABILITY IN AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT MISSION RELIABILITY IN AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English-language Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Micro/Nanorobot Fabrication and Regenerative Biomanufacturing Sixty-Flagship series (Flagship 50/60). It investigates safe failure recovery with preserved productive service. The research coupling is autonomous manufacturing mission x regenerative specimen integrity x physically verified fault recovery. All proposed work is restricted to nonclinical in-vitro, organ-on-chip, synthetic phantom or authorized ex-vivo environments. No experiments were executed in preparing this edition; no human treatment, clinical efficacy or regulatory clearance is claimed. Its falsifiable candidate is: A frozen safety and recovery protocol will improve completed qualified work at equal fault burden while meeting independent stop and specimen integrity gates. The Atlas minimum demonstrator is: Blind-inject four fault classes into complete cell assembly missions with matched useful work targets. Strong comparators include expert human operation, fixed automation scripts and conventional redundant hardware. A central rival account is apparent safety caused by aborting early and completing less useful work. The nonnegotiable stop condition is: no advantage at equal effective work or an unknown fault fails to stop the apparatus. Each failed, aborted, hidden-fault and incomplete run is retained in the experimental denominator, and observation of a finished form is never substituted for independently measured function. Thirty mathematical plates address domain-specific metrics and established model families across transport, measurement, elasticity, time-dependent dynamics, causal attribution, calibration and uncertainty. Eighty-two chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations organize six research arcs. Two hundred Research Gates have been revised with independent observables, one of fifteen blinded causal intervention families, orthogonal controls and noncompensatory refusal criteria. Thirty mathematical plates now carry model-specific physical derivation commentary, explicit applicability limits and distinct flagship-level blind checks. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose unbuilt future instruments and succession artifacts, each requiring its own bench validation. This version is a research design and not a report of validated physical findings. It draws scientific method and conceptual boundaries from the user-supplied Atlas and research mother volumes; especially the Atlas-supplied ancestry DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020. Full external bibliographic DOI checking and scientific peer review have not been completed. Domain-specific sensitivity, causal identifiability and independent replication require qualified laboratory evaluation before any scientific superiority claim. items.summary: Industrial Screw Driving Datasets This comprehensive dataset collection captures time-series data from industrial screw driving operations in plastic components. Designed for research in manufacturing process monitoring, anomaly detection, and quality control, it includes over 34,000 individual screw driving operations across six distinct scenarios. Each scenario investigates specific aspects of the screw driving process, from natural wear patterns to controlled material variations. Overview Scenario name Observations Classes Purpose s01_variations-in-thread-degradation  5,000  1 Studies natural degradation of plastic threads over repeated use cycles, documenting wear patterns and failure progression s02_variations-in-surface-friction 12,500  8 Examines effects of different surface conditions (lubricants, surface treatments, contamination) on screw driving performance s03_variations-in-assembly-conditions-1  1,700 26 Investigates diverse component and assembly faults including washer modifications, thread deformations, and alignment issues s04_variations-in-assembly-conditions-2  5,000 25 Features methodically arranged assembly fault conditions in 5 distinct error groups with paired normal/abnormal operations s05_variations-in-upper-workpiece-fabrication  2,400 42 Analyzes how injection molding parameter variations in the upper component affect screw driving metrics s06_variations-in-lower-workpiece-fabrication  7,482 44 Explores effects of injection molding parameter variations in the lower component on fastening quality Experimental Setup Automatic screwing station (EV motor control unit assembly) Delta PT 40x12 screws optimized for thermoplastics Target torque: 1.4 Nm (range: 1.2-1.6 Nm) Sampling frequency: 833.33 Hz Data completeness: >95% Detailed time-series measurements including torque, angle, gradient, and time values Dataset Features These datasets are suitable for various research purposes. Each ZIP file contains:  Complete raw data in JSON format for maximum flexibility Standardized labels.csv files for metadata and classification Comprehensive README.md documentation for each scenario Various error classes with varying degrees of severity Time series data for the complete screwing process Research Applications Development of machine learning models for anomaly detection Process monitoring and quality control system development Manufacturing analytics and parameter optimization Digital twin development for screw driving operations Material property influences on assembly processes Access and Usage For data handling, we recommend our  PyScrew Python package ( https://github.com/nikolaiwest/pyscrew ). However, this is optional: The data is easily accessible using standard JSON and CSV processing. No changes were made to the raw data and all information on the experiments can be found in the labels.csv file.  Citation Request When using this dataset in academic work, please cite this project or the mentioned papers from the README.md files. items.summary: YAHIQ 31.16     English Launch Text for Zendo Here are the three sections in English, written to be posted on Zendo. I kept the tone technical but accessible, and made sure nothing claims more than the code actually does.   1) What's New in 31.16 YAHIQ 31.16     From Numeric Memory to Dual Polar Coordinates YAHIQ has traveled a clear path: from the Fibonacci word bank, to the Kaaf-Ha-Ya-Ain-Sad heartbeat, to the rotating dhikr cycle     and now to a new mathematical layer. Version 31.16 brings three structural changes: A) Dual polar coordinates for every word.  A word is no longer just a "code." It is a complex number:         where  n  is the word's numeric code and   is its internal phase. That phase comes from a dual mapping: for bank records,  Fibonacci + phonetic ; for input text,  the fourth key + phonetic . The result: every word is a point on the complex plane, not just a number on a line. B) The sentence equation.  A sentence is no longer a simple sum of codes. Each sentence gets a state vector: and sentence coherence is measured from the sum of phase differences between consecutive pairs: This means YAHIQ can report  how internally consistent a sentence is     without claiming to have definitively understood its meaning. C) Strict layer separation.  The YSSE sentence engine, the equation analyzer, the verse tester, and the chat each have their own independent memory and keys. Changing one does not touch the others. LIFECYCLE AND SUSTAINABILITY ENGINEERING FOR NANOROBOT-ASSISTED REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates functional-unit normalized whole-system material and energy accounting. Its scientific coupling is biomanufacturing x resource efficiency x life-cycle governance. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Does microrobotic manufacture reduce cradle-to-disposal resources per independently function-qualified tissue unit rather than shifting burdens to computing or consumables? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Meter complete energy and consumables for a small-batch robotic and conventional tissue manufacturing comparison. Strong comparators include conventional bioprinting and centralized regulated-grade benchmark workflows. The central competing explanation is hidden reagent, compute or cold-chain displacement beyond the declared factory boundary. The noncompensatory stop rule is: material boundary is incomplete or advantage disappears per qualified functional unit. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. items.summary: This document is the supplementary technical appendix to the paper "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks." This appendix collects the mathematical proofs and technical details that could not be included in the main paper due to page limitations. It covers the proof of Lemma 1 (privacy), Lemma 2 (participation), and Theorem 1 (mean-squared error guarantee). The appendix additionally provides a bound for the geometric-median aggregator, including its corresponding mean-squared error analysis; the optimization problem underlying the relay weights described in Section VI; and illustrative worked examples. The proof of Theorem 1 does not assume that honest Stage-1 outputs remain within a prescribed radius, accounting instead for their second-moment contribution and deriving the variance of the honest-only estimator explicitly. Finally, numerical checks of the theoretical lemmas and bounds are presented, together with supplementary assumptions, analytical details, and discussions supporting the results in the main paper. This appendix is intended to serve as a technical reference for the mathematical analysis and theoretical guarantees of BRICER.
items.title: Appendix to "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks"

items.summary: Extending Granger causality to tell a direct link from a hidden common cause: the earlier signal is whitened on the joint past, then a rank-based HCR test of residual independence with calibrated p-values is applied, which works when the innovations are non-Gaussian. Includes a one-file Python tool, a browser version, and checks on synthetic data, rivers, stock returns and microservice incidents.

items.summary: Pre-registered audit of twelve open-weight language models (Chinese, American, European, Thai and Korean) run locally with Ollama on a 240-prompt factorial design: investor nationality × prompt language × risk tolerance × horizon × template. Each model allocates 100% across eight equity markets. The archive holds the research note ( paper/paper.pdf ), the pre-analysis plan, the prompt set, all raw replies, the parsed panel, the estimation code and the generated tables and figures. Every number in the note is rebuilt from the cached replies with make all . Headline result: with the prompt held fixed, a model's home market receives −0.42 pp (95% CI −0.59 to −0.25) relative to what models of other origins give it, so the pre-registered home-bias hypothesis is not supported. The investor's stated country of residence moves allocations by +1.88 pp, about four times the absolute size of the home effect. Licences: code and text Apache-2.0; prompt set, parsed tables and documentation CC BY 4.0; model outputs remain subject to the licence of the model that generated them.
items.title: Do Open-Source LLMs Have a Home Bias? Investment Advice from Chinese, American, European and Thai Models (research note, replies dataset and code)

items.summary: Harris's inequality states that increasing functions of independent $\pm1$ variables are positively correlated. We record a sharpening that is linear in a single Fourier--Walsh coefficient: under any product measure the covariance of two increasing functions is at least $\max_i\hat f(\{i\})\hat g(\{i\})$, and under the uniform measure this maximum equals $\max_{T\neq\emptyset}|\hat f(T)\hat g(T)|$, so the covariance dominates the negative part of any single spectral term. The analogue with a sum over coordinates fails, and under a biased product measure the single-term form can fail; for $n=3$ and $n=4$ it holds precisely when the bias parameter lies in $[\frac14,\frac34]$. We apply the inequality to pure $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge theory. Gauge invariance reduces the law of the four links of a plaquette to a one-parameter family indexed by the plaquette expectation $m$, and we show that the minimal covariance of increasing $[0,1]$-valued functions of these links equals $-m/8$. Consequently the link measure is not positively associated at any positive coupling, is not a coordinatewise increasing function of independent variables, and is not stochastically increasing in the coupling. For increasing functions of more links the value $-m/8$ can be exceeded: on the $2^3$ torus a pair of functions of four links each reaches $-\frac{33}{256}$ as $\beta\to\infty$.
items.title: A ONE-COEFFICIENT SHARPENING OF HARRIS'S INEQUALITY, AND OPTIMAL NEGATIVE ASSOCIATION IN Z2 LATTICE GAUGE THEORY

items.summary: Abstract and Prior-Art Disclosure This manuscript serves as a formal public prior-art disclosure, conceptual research archive, and consolidated technical design dossier for the proposed Metric Spacetime Manipulator 26 (MSM-26) architecture. As the twenty-sixth revision and direct successor to MSM-25 Rev. 3, MSM-26 preserves the established architectural topology, chronological provenance, authorship, foundational subsystem configurations, and speculative physical mechanisms of the continuing Metric Spacetime Manipulator research program, while introducing substantial refinements to its flux-bias architecture, resonator construction, electromagnetic coupling configurations, operating principles, and associated engineering specifications. This revision supersedes MSM-25 Rev. 3 and all preceding MSM revisions, except where earlier configurations are explicitly retained as architectural inheritance or documented in the revision-comparison, errata, and reconciliation registers. MSM-26 specifies a cryogenic superconducting architecture whose active core consists of a closed, series-connected chain of Superconducting Nonlinear Asymmetric Inductive eLement (SNAIL) fluxonium cells , collectively designated the SNAILonium. Adjacent galvanically connected SNAIL elements possess alternating loop chirality, with each element incorporating exactly (n=3) large Josephson junctions and an associated small Josephson junction. The architecture retains its admissible superconducting conductor configurations, comprising the superconducting flat-wire ribbon and the contour-conformal coplanar-waveguide configuration, with the latter incorporating ground-plane boundaries that follow the SNAIL contour and locally widened gaps around the junction regions. The Josephson-junction interlayer retains three admissible configurations: a conventional dielectric insulating barrier, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, and moiré-twisted (MoTe_2). The architecture retains three principal SNAILonium lumped-element resonance circuit configurations: the ring-shaped resonator, the flat bifilar Fermat spiral terminating in two tangentially and galvanically coupled SNAILonium rings, and the bifilar poloidal–toroidal helix arranged along closed toroidal geodesics. The third configuration further incorporates a dedicated second filar functioning concurrently as a flux-bias line and kinetic inductance resonator. This revision substantially develops that dual-function subsystem into a three-construction architecture comprising (a) a superconducting split-ring resonator formed from a capacitive-gap-interrupted flat-wire ribbon; (b) a coplanar-strip (CPS) resonator, newly introduced in MSM-26, with one or both superconducting strips interrupted by transverse capacitive gaps arranged in-line or offset by (90^\circ); and (c) a coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonator incorporating in-line capacitive gaps in its ground-plane rings. The capacitive discontinuities may be implemented using vacuum air-bridge or interdigital capacitors. All three constructions are broadside coupled to the superconducting SNAILonium conductor carrying the (n=3) large junctions. Beyond specifying these three constructions, MSM-26 develops their associated electromagnetic operating characteristics, including the common and staggered flux-response patterns, coplanar-strip odd- and even-mode field configurations, gap-dependent fundamental-mode selection, distributed resonator behaviour, and the concurrent flux-biasing and kinetic-inductance-resonance functions. The revised architecture also incorporates the flux-biasing superconducting Helmholtz superinductor pair, providing the global magnetic-flux-biasing configuration, alongside the ring-level and strut-level flux-bias subsystems.
